```{r}
set.seed(13012021) 
z.conf.int<-function(sample.mean,sigma,n,level=0.95){ 
  margin<-sigma*qnorm(1-(1-level)/2)/sqrt(n); 
  c(sample.mean-margin,sample.mean+margin)
}
t.conf.int<-function(sample.mean,sigma,n,level=0.95){ 
  margin<-sigma*qt(1-(1-level)/2,n-1)/sqrt(n);
  c(sample.mean-margin,sample.mean+margin)
}
```  

# Exercise 1
## a)
Since the standard deviation was estimated from the same sample, we use the $t$-distribution:
```{r}
onecinema<-t.conf.int(25467,4980,100)
onecinema
```
## b)
```{r}
total<-3672*onecinema
total/10^6
```
## c)  
As the lower bound of the confidence interval is $89.88$ million, which is greater than $72$ million, we can confidently say that the record was broken.

# Exercise 2

The null hypothesis is that $X\sim\mathcal{N}(34.2,\sigma^2)$. As $\sigma^2$ is not known, we need to use the $t$-test. The (two-tailed) $p$-value is
```{r}
heads<-scan("heads.csv",sep=",")
2*pt(abs((mean(heads)-34.2)/(sd(heads)/sqrt(length(heads)))),length(heads)-1,lower.tail=FALSE)
```
We can also use the R command for $t$-test:
```{r}
t.test(heads,mu=34.2)
```
The $p$-value is less than $3$%, so we can reject the null hypothesis at the standard $5$% significance level. It is reasonable to conclude that the population mean head circumference is different from $34.2$cm.

# Exercise 3
Let $\mu$ be the actual average level to which the machine fills the cartoons. 

## Confidence interval

Let's calculate the $95$% lower confidence bound for $\mu$ (that is, we use a method that will give a number smaller than $\mu$ for $95$% of samples) given that the standard deviation is $0.03$:
```{r}
sugar<-scan("sugar.csv",sep=",")
mean(sugar) - 0.03*qnorm(0.95)/sqrt(length(sugar))
```
It is greater than $1$, so the machine is indeed overfilling the cartons (save for a less than $5$% chance of an usual sample).

## Hypothesis test
We want to obtain evidence that the machine is overfilling the cartons, 
hence we will try to reject the hypothesis that $\mu\le 1$.
The null hypothesis is that $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,0.03^2)$, $\mu\le1$.
We need to calculate the upper-tail probability, hence the $p$-value for $\mu=1$ is
```{r}
sugar<-scan("sugar.csv",sep=",")
pnorm((mean(sugar)-1)/(0.03/sqrt(length(sugar))),lower.tail=FALSE)
```
The $p$-value is less then $0.001$%, so we reject the null hypothesis with a very high confidence.

# Exercise 4
The null hypothesis is that $X\sim\mathcal{N}(7.6,0.707)$. The (two-tailed) $p$-value is 
```{r}
water<-scan("water.csv",sep=",")
2*pnorm(abs((mean(water)-7.6)/(0.707/sqrt(length(water)))),lower.tail=FALSE)
```
The $p$-value is quite large, so there is no reason to reject the null hypothesis.

# Exercise 5
If $25$ is the median indeed, then $X\sim B(20,0.5)$.

## a) 
Type I error is the probability to reject the null hypothesis wrongly, so the probability of Type I error is calculated assuming that $X\sim B(20,0.5)$ and equal to $\Pr[X\le 4\text{ or }X\ge 16]$:
```{r}
pbinom(4,20,0.5)+pbinom(15,20,0.5,FALSE)
```

## b)
Since $\Pr[X\le\delta] = \Pr[X\ge 20-\delta]$, we need to find $\delta$ such that $\Pr[X\le\delta]\le0.025$:
```{r}
qbinom(0.025,20,0.5) - 1
```   
We subtract $1$ because `qbinom` produces the smallest value of $x$ such that $\Pr[X\le x]$ is not less than the given threshold. For a discrete distribution like binomial, this makes an important difference as illustrated below:
```{r}
pbinom(6,20,0.5)
pbinom(5,20,0.5)
```   

## c) 

Let's now count $Y$, the number of observed lifetimes which are less than $25$ hours. 
If the true median lifetime is $25$ hours, then $Y\sim B(20,0.5)$ as before.
If the true median is greater than $25$ hours, then $Y\sim B(20,p)$ with some $p<0.5$.

Consider the probability $\Pr[Y\ge 20 - \delta]$. We can calculate it for $Y\sim B(20,0.5)$.
If $Y\sim B(20,p)$ with some $p<0.5$, the probability $\Pr[Y\ge 20 - \delta]$ will be smaller.
Hence, if the value of $\delta$ is such that $\Pr[Y\ge 20 - \delta]$ is small for $Y\sim B(20,0.5)$,
then $\Pr[Y\ge 20 - \delta]$ will also be small for $Y\sim B(20,p)$ with any $p<0.5$.

Let $y$ be the observed number  of lifetimes less then $25$ hours.
The testing procedure is as follows: reject the hypothesis that the median lifetime is at least $25$ hours
if $y \le 20 - \delta$. An appropriate value of $\delta$ is selected to guarantee the desired 
significance similarly to (b) above.


# Exercise 6

We assess whether the goal scoring ability of a ``typical player'' changes.
```{r}
library(Hmisc)
bask <- spss.get("basketball.sav")
t.test(bask$BEFORE - bask$AFTER,mu=0)
t.test(bask$BEFORE,bask$AFTER,paired=TRUE) # a different interface to the same test
```   
The p-value is barely significant. We have some evidence that the goal scoring ability changes.

Remark: if the data had been the scores of two different players, we would have not obtained any significant difference:
```{r}
t.test(bask$BEFORE,bask$AFTER)
```   
However, removing just one point looking like an outlier makes the difference significant:
```{r}
t.test(bask$BEFORE,bask$AFTER[-4])
```   

# Exercise 7

The recorded levels from the same site vary significantly, and the calendar gives us a natural matching,
so we will look how the difference between the two sites changes.
```{r}
phos <- read.csv("phosphorus.csv")
t.test(phos$Site.1-phos$Site.2,mu=0)
```   
The p-value is quite small, hence there is a significant difference between the two sites.

# Exercise 8 

10 unrelated plants of each species were selected, so we use a two-samples test.
```{r}
seaweed <- read.csv("seaweed.csv")
t.test(seaweed$Spiralis,seaweed$Serratus)
```  
No evidence of significant difference.
